property_summary: After calling go() with some value, the owner address (via c.owner()) receives exactly that value from the contract (address(c).balance becomes 0 and owner balance increases by the sent amount).

For every call to go() with any payable amount and any recipient contract at the fixed target address, the reference always leaves C with zero balance after forwarding remaining balance to owner via transfer (so address(c).balance == 0), whereas the mutant that uses call to send to owner can leave non-zero balance when owner is a contract whose fallback/receive reverts or consumes gas differently causing the call to fail and revert the send (breaking the guarantee).

For every caller and payable amount, after C.go(...) completes the correct contract forwards its entire balance out so address(c).balance == 0; replacing transfer with call allows the owner-send to fail when owner is a contract that reverts on receive, leaving address(c).balance > 0 for some inputs (owner as reverting contract).

For every payable call to go(targetContract, value) the reference C always leaves its own balance zero after completion (it forwards remaining balance to owner using transfer), but the mutant that uses call to send to owner can fail to forward (if owner is a contract whose receive/fallback reverts), leaving C with non-zero balance for some inputs.

For every caller and payable amount, after calling go() the reference contract always allows the send to owner to revert the whole transaction if the owner reverts (so go() never completes successfully when owner refuses funds), whereas the mutant using call may succeed the outer call while the owner-send fails (or vice versa) leading to differing completion/revert behavior; the test asserts that go() always reverts when owner is a contract whose receive() always reverts (reference: transfer causes revert, mutant: call returns false and is reverted by our try/catch observation).

For any caller and any payable amount, when the contract's owner is an address that accepts funds, calling go(...) always completes successfully and leaves C with zero balance; if the owner is a contract that intentionally reverts on receiving funds, the reference C's transfer will cause the entire go() to revert (so the external call fails), while the mutant using call can return control (or fail differently) causing a different observable outcome — we assert that when owner is a reverting contract, calling go() reverts (reference holds for all inputs, mutant is broken for some inputs).

For any payable call to go() that forwards ETH to an external target which may accept the funds, the contract C MUST preserve owner (owner stays the deployer) after go() completes; the mutant replaces the final transfer with resetting owner, so owner can change to zero address for some inputs.

For any caller and any amount of ether sent to C.go, the reference contract always forwards the received ether to the hard-coded target address (so the final balance of C is zero and owner receives the funds), while the mutant that calls the target with value 0 can leave ether in C and thus can change address(c).balance/owner payout for some inputs (e.g., when the target would have accepted funds).

For any caller and any nonzero ETH amount sent to C.go, the reference forwards that ETH to the hard-coded target so C's balance is always zero after go() (owner receives funds); the mutant sending zero value to the target can leave ETH in C, so for some fuzzed amount and adversarial target behavior the mutant results in address(c).balance > 0 while the reference always has address(c).balance == 0.

For every caller and ETH amount, C.go always forwards the received ETH to the hard-coded target which (when it accepts) results in address(c).balance == 0 after the call; the mutant that calls the target with value 0 can leave ETH in C so address(c).balance > 0 for some inputs (fuzzer will find an amount and an accepting helper to make the mutant fail this property).

For any caller and any nonnegative ETH amount sent to C.go, the reference forwards the received ETH to the hard-coded target so that C's balance is zero after go() (assertTrue(address(c).balance == 0)); the mutant that calls the target with value 0 can leave ETH in C so address(c).balance > 0 for some fuzzed amount when the target accepts funds, breaking the rule.

For any caller and any nonzero ether amount sent into C.go, the correct contract forwards that ether onward (so C's balance remains zero after go), while the mutant that calls the target with value 0 can leave ether stuck in C causing address(c).balance > 0 for some fuzzed amount and an accepting callee — the test asserts address(c).balance == 0 (holds for reference for all inputs) and the mutant will fail it for some inputs.

For any nonzero wei sent into go() where the external target call succeeds, the reference contract always forwards the full contract balance to owner after go() returns; the mutant sends only half the balance for some inputs, violating this rule.

After any call to go() that sends nonzero wei to a callee which accepts the funds, the contract forwards its entire balance to owner (reference) — the mutant forwards only half the balance for some inputs, so the owner's received balance can be strictly less than the contract's pre-transfer balance.

For any caller and any nonzero ETH amount sent into go(target) where the target accepts the low-level call, the reference C forwards its entire remaining balance to owner after go() returns; the mutant forwards only half the balance for some inputs, so owner receives less than the contract balance in those cases.

For any nonzero ETH value sent into go() to a callee that accepts the forwarded call, the reference contract always forwards its entire balance to owner after go() returns; the mutant sometimes forwards only half, so owner receives less than the contract balance.

After calling go() with any nonzero ETH amount to a callee that accepts the funds, the reference contract always forwards its entire remaining balance to owner (so owner ends up with the ETH sent), whereas the mutant sometimes forwards only half the contract balance, causing owner to receive less than the forwarded ETH.
